Figure 1. (a) Sketch map of the Central Asian Orogenic Belt showing main blocks, suture zones and Mesozoic aged strike-slip faults (Modified after Huang
et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2017; Xiao et al., 2018). The Amuria block, including the Songliao, Jiamusi, and Mongolia blocks, is shown in brown to denote its extent.
Distributions of Hegenshan Ophiolites are shown in green. Distribution of flora and other fauna are after Shen et al. (2006), Wang et al. (2013), Yan et al. (2019)
and Niu et al. (2021). Abbreviations are: NHS, Nenjiang-Heihe Suture; ES, Erlianhot Suture; SMXB, South Mongolia-Xing'an Belt. (b) Geological map of the
sampling locality (modified after 1:200, 000 scale geological map in IMBGMR, 1991).
of Amuria prior to the amalgamation of the Songliao-Jiamusi and Mongolia blocks. Thus, timing the final
closure of the Nenjiang Ocean as well as the final unification of Amuria are critical for understanding the
Phanerozoic evolution of the PAO and the geodynamic evolution of the Asian blocks in Pangea.
Previous studies posit that the final closure of the Nenjiang Ocean occurred sometime between the Early
Devonian to Early Triassic (e.g., Han et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2017, 2019; Ma et al., 2020; Miao et al., 2004;
Zhao et al., 2010, 2014; Zhang, 2013; Xu et al., 2015). Those studies exclusively relied on the geological
evidence for closure such as stratigraphy and the geochemistry of affiliated ophiolites and igneous rocks;
however, only limited paleomagnetic data are available to quantify the age of final closure.
Paleomagnetism is the principal tool to constrain spatio-temporal movements of continents. A paleomag-
netic approach allows for the direct comparison of coeval paleolatitudinal data from the two blocks to date
the final closure of the Nenjiang Ocean. Numerous paleomagnetic studies on the Permo-Carboniferous

Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 10.1029/2021JB022881
strata have been carried out from different tectonic units of the Mongolia block, namely the Gurvansayhan
(Bazhenov et al., 2016; Kovalenko & Chernov, 2008; Kovalenko, 2010), Uliastai-Xing'an (Chen et al., 1997;
Li et al., 2012; Zhang, Huang, Zhao, & Zhang, 2018; Zhang et al., 2021) and Erguna (Pruner, 1987, 1992; Xu
et al., 1997; Kravchinsky, Cogne et al., 2002, Kravchinsky, Sorokin, 2002; Zhao et al., 2020). These studies
provide constraints on the paleoposition of Mongolia through time, but no quality paleomagnetic data are
available for the Songliao-Jiamusi block.
In this contribution, we present the first Permo-Carboniferous paleomagnetic data from the Songliao-Ji-
amusi block, aiming to effectively constrain its paleoposition with respect to Mongolia and assess the con-
figuration of Amuria during the late Paleozoic. We summarize the tectonic evolution of the PAO and pro-
pose a comprehensive reconstruction model for the CAOB at the Permo-Carboniferous boundary.
2. Geological Setting and Sampling
The CAOB is the largest accretionary orogenic belt sandwiched between the Siberia, Baltica and Tarim-North
China cratons (Figure 1a; Han & Zhao, 2018; Han et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2017; Wilhem et al., 2012; Wind-
ley et al., 2007; Xiao et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2015). The eastern part of the CAOB is comprised of Mongolia,
Songliao, Jiamusi and Xilinhot blocks. The Precambrian basement floored Erguna terrane occupies the
northern part of the Mongolia block whereas the southern region borders a Carboniferous active conti-
nental margin known as the South Mongolia-Xing'an Belt (SMXB), or Gurvansayhan, Uliastai and Xing'an
blocks in previous studies (Figure 1a; Badarch et al., 2002; Eizenhöfer & Zhao, 2018; Liu et al., 2017; Zhang,
Huang, Zhao, Meert, et al., 2018, 2021). The Songliao and Jiamusi blocks were amalgamated before the Ear-
ly Devonian (Liu et al., 2019; Meng et al., 2010) and separated again in the Late Permian (Zhu et al., 2017).
The unified Songliao-Jiamusi block collided with the Mongolia block along the Nenjiang-Heihe Suture
(NHS) and with North China along the Solonker Suture sometime during the late Paleozoic (Figure 1a; Liu
et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2015). The Xilinhot block is situated to the north of the SMXB along the Erlianhot
Suture and to the south by the North China block along the Solonker Suture (Figure 1a; Liu et al., 2017).
The exact boundary defining the limits of the Xilinhot and Songliao blocks remains cryptic due to limited
geological evidence (Figure 1a, Liu et al., 2019).
The western margin of the Songliao-Jiamusi block developed on Precambrian basement whereas the interi-
or Songliao basin is floored by Mesozoic and late Paleozoic basement (Qian et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2018). Si-
lurian to Carboniferous arc-related igneous rocks that recorded bilateral subduction of the Nenjiang Ocean
are preserved on both sides of the NHS (Feng et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2020). A suite of Upper
Carboniferous to Upper Permian volcanic-sedimentary sequences outcrop in the Ulanhot area (Figures 1b
and 2; IMBGMR, 1991). From oldest to youngest, the Upper Carboniferous to Lower Permian Dashizhai
Formation comprises neritic basic to felsic lavas, tuffs and interbedded sandstones with abundant branchi-
opod and Crinoid fossils (Neospirifer sp., Schizophoria sp.); the Lower-Middle Permian Zhesi Formation
includes the previously defined Wujiatun Formation and consists of slates, bioclastic limestones, shales and
sandstones, developing branchiopods, reefs, crinoides and bryozoans; the Upper Permian Linxi Formation
comprises slates, sandstones and interbedded felsic volcaniclastic rocks with abundant bivalves and the
Angara genus of phytoliths (IMBGMR, 1991). The tectonic setting for the mafic to felsic volcanic rocks of
the Dashizhai Formation are debated with some favoring a rift environment (Zeng et al., 2011) and others
arguing that the rocks are subduction-related (Li, 2013; Zhang, 2013). This disparity in classification is one
of the main reasons that there is controversy in establishing the age of suturing of the NHS.
We collected 15 sites (154 specimens) of basalts and andesites from the type section of the Dashizhai For-
mation in the Dashizhai area (Figures 1b, 2, and Figures S1a–S1b in Supporting Information S1). Most
interbedded sandstones are strongly weathered or thin-layered, thus they are discarded from sampling.
We collected two sites (21 specimens) from the sandstones of the Zhesi Formation in the Haoren area
(Figures 1b, 2 and Figure S1c in Supporting Information S1) as the remaining section appeared to be signifi-
cantly altered and deformed. In the Suolun area, we collected eight sites (84 specimens) from the sandstones
of the Linxi Formation (Figures 1b, 2 and Figure S1d in Supporting Information S1). All cores were drilled
using a portable paleomagnetic drill and oriented using magnetic and/or sun compass (Table 1 and Table S2

### page_5
Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 10.1029/2021JB022881
in Supporting Information S1). To better constrain the eruption age of our sampling lavas, we collected a
dacitic andesite sample (MD43) for zircon U-Pb dating.
3. Methods
We applied heavy liquid and magnetic separation techniques to filter out zircon separation in sample MD43
and purified them by handpicking use a binocular microscope, then we captured Cathodoluminescence
(CL) images using a JSM-6510 Scanning Electron Microscope to display the internal structures of zircon
grains. Zircon U-Pb isotopes were analyzed at the Department of Geological Sciences, University of Florida
using a “Nu-Plasma HR” laser ablation multi-collector inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometer (LA-
MC-ICP-MS) equipped with 213 nm tandem Applied Spectra laser. Each acquisition incorporated 20 s back-
ground and followed a 30 s ablation (30 μm spot size) on zircon grains using Argon and Helium as carrier
gas. FC-1 (1099.0 ± 0.7 Ma) zircons were used as external standards for calibration (Black et al., 2003). Raw
data reduction was processed with a spreadsheet CALAMARI and diagrams were generated using Isoplot
(Ludwig, 2003). Analytical data are summarized in Table S1 in Supporting Information S1.
We cut all oriented core specimens into 2.2 × 2.5 cm standard size and selected pilot samples from each
sampling section for rock magnetic analysis. Hysteresis loops, Isothermal Remanent Magnetization (IRM)
acquisitions and back-field demagnetization of saturated IRM (SIRM) were analyzed using a Micromag
3900 Vibrating Sample Magnetometer at University of Florida. The andesite sample MD42-8 was subjected
to a magnetization-temperature dependence experiment using a variable field translation balance at the
Institute of Geology and Geophysics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (IGGCAS). We then carried out
stepwise thermal and/or alternating field demagnetization (>15 steps) on all core specimens to isolate char-
acteristic remanent magnetizations (ChRMs) at IGGCAS (sites MD35-43) and the Magnetotectonics Lab
of Peking University (sites MD144–149). Both labs are magnetically shielded rooms with residual field less
than 300 nT. For each demagnetization step, cores were heated in an ASC TD48-SC oven (internal field less
than 10 nT), then measured using a 2G-755 superconducting rock magnetometer. Remanence components
were isolated using principal component analysis (Kirschvink, 1980). Fisherian statistics were calculat-
ed using PMGSC (Enkin et al., 2003), Pmagpy (Tauxe et al., 2016) and/or paleomagnetism.org (Koymans
et al., 2020) for crosscheck.
4. Results
4.1. Zircon U-Pb Dating
CL images display well-developed oscillatory zonation for most zircon grains of dacitic andesite sample
(MD43), which are euhedral crystals with lengths range from 50 to 150 μm and length/width ratios of 3:2 to
3:1 (Figure 3a). Zircon grains with discordant values (>5%) were excluded from mean calculation. A total of
29 concordant analysis of zircon separations generated 206Pb/238U ages of 288–300 Ma and yielded a weight-
ed mean age of 291.8 ± 2.1 Ma (MSWD = 0.4, n = 29; Figure 3b).
4.2. Rock Magnetism
Magnetic signals of the sandstones from the Linxi (ML28-5) and Zhesi (MZ33-8) formations are relatively
weak (Figures 4a–4f). Hysteresis loops are nearly reversible and fully saturated before 0.4 T (Figures 4a
and 4d). The B and B values are very low and SIRM values are less than 3 × 10−8 Am2/kg (Figures 4a, 4b,
c cr
4d and 4e). Values of M /M and B /B are 0.04–0.09 and 3.06–4.67 respectively, indicating magnetite sizes
rs s cr c
near pseudo-single domain (PSD) to multi-domain (MD) (Dunlop, 2002). Component analysis of IRM ac-
quisition (Kruiver et al., 2001) yielded inconclusive results due to the noisy signal (Figures 4c and 4f). These
indicate that the dominant magnetic carrier in the sandstones is low coercivity magnetite.
Magnetization-temperature dependence curve for the andesite sample (MD42-8) from the Dashizhai For-
mation is not fully reversible for the heating and cooling curves before 530 °C. In the heating process,
the magnetization slightly decreases before 530 °C, followed by a rap∼id decrease up to 585 °C (Fig-
ure 4h). The hysteresis loop is narrow and esse∼ntially saturated at 0.4 T (Figure 4g). The SIRM∼ values reach-
es 6 × 10−6 Am2/kg. Values of M /M and B /B are 0.12 and 4.11 respectively, suggesting a PSD state of

Figure 3. (a) Cathodoluminescence images of representative zircon grains from the dacitic andesites (MD43) of the Dashizhai Formation, showing 206Pb/238U
ages of each analyzed spot; (b) U-Pb concordia diagram and weighted mean age plot.
magnetite (Figures 4g and 4i; Dunlop, 2002). Component analysis isolated three end-members including
the low coercivity component (39.8 mT), intermediate coercivity component (107.2 mT) and high coercivity
component (708.0 mT) (Figure 4j; Kruiver et al., 2001). The above analyses indicate magnetite is the domi-
nant magnetic carrier of the lavas in the Dashizhai Formation. A minor high coercivity component can be
attributed to hematite formed by deuteric oxidation during lava cooling.
4.3. Paleomagnetism
The low temperature components (LTCs) of sandstones from the Linxi Formation were typically removed
before 530°C (Figures 5a and 5b). Remanences are unstable after removal of LTCs (Figure 5b) and no stable
ChRMs were isolated from these samples. Demagnetization of sandstones from the Zhesi Formation isolat-
ed single component, which were typically eliminated before 350°C and pointed to the origin (Figure 5c).
The LTCs from both formations are close to the present geomagnetic field and indicative of a possibly recent
overprint. Results from the Linxi and Zhesi formations are discarded for further analysis.
We identified two components in most lava samples of the Dashizhai Formation (Figures 5e–5n). The
low stability components are scattered and typically removed by 250–450°C and 10 mT. Well-determined
ChRMs were typically isolated between 500–560°C and 15–100 mT from at least four steps. We accepted the
best resolved ChRMs with maximum angular deviation less than 15° then converted them to specimen-level
VGPs (Table S2 in Supporting Information S1). Two types of cutoffs were applied to the VGPs, namely the
fixed −45° and Vandamme cutoffs (Vandamme, 1994), and generated almost identical screening results. We
chose the fixed −45° cutoff to filter out the most reliable data for further statistics (Figures 6a–6c; Table S2
in Supporting Information S1). Specimen-level mean ChRMs is calculated from the Fisher mean of VGPs
and evaluated for paleosecular variation (PSV) of geomagnetic field using the N-dependent A -envelope
95
test (Deenen et al., 2011). The mean ChRMs calculated from 116 out of 154 specimen-level VGPs is Dg/
Ig = 60.7°/−77.7°, k = 5.0, α = 6.6° before and Ds/Is = 20.3°/−45.9°, k = 31.1, α = 2.4° after tilt correc-
g 95 s 95
tion (Figures 6b and 6c). The A value falls into the N-dependent envelope (A min = 1.8° < A = 2.4°<
95 95 95
A max = 4.1°, N = 116, K = 30.4; Figure 6a; Table S2 in Supporting Information S1), indicating an averaged
95
PSV in our data set. Data with negative inclinations were inverted and compared with the positive group.
Both groups share a common true mean from 1000 bootstrapped Cartesian coordinates at 95% confidence
(Figure 7; Tauxe, 2010), indicative of a positive reversal test. We also calculated the site-mean direction of
ChRMs with Dg/Ig = 70.6°/−77.5°, k = 4.8, α = 21.2° before and Ds/Is = 20.6°/-46.6°, k = 55.7, α = 5.4°
g 95 s 95
after tilt correction (N = 13 sites; Figures 6d and 6f; Table 1). Overall clustering improves after tilt correc-
tion with k/k = 11.66 > F (13, 13) = 1.98, suggesting a positive fold test at 95% confidence limit (Table 1; s g

The Dashizhai Formation sensu lato is outcrops throughout the Songliao and Xilinhot blocks. Previous
geochronological data yield a broad range in ages between 274 Ma to 313 Ma (Li, 2013). In the type sec-
tion of the Dashizhai Formation where we sampled, two weighted mean ages from dacites were dated to
294 ± 2 Ma (Zhang, 2013) and 313 ± 2 Ma (Zeng et al., 2011). Our zircon U-Pb dating for the dacitic andesite
(MD43) yielded an age of 291.8 ± 2.8 Ma. Our sampling therefore spans an interval between 292–313 Ma

In sum, the ChRMs acquired from the 302.5 ± 10.5 Ma volcanics of the Dashizhai Formation are very likely
primary records of geomagnetic field with positive fold, reversal and PSV tests. A corresponding paleomag-
netic pole is then calculated at P = 12.8°S, P = 102.4°E (A = 5.4°, N = 13 sites; Table 1).

5. Discussion
The R-criteria (Meert et al., 2020) was advocated to evaluate the reliability of paleomagnetic poles. Our
new pole meets six out of seven R-criteria, including: (R1) well determined rock age that constrained to
within ±15 Ma (302.5 ± 10.5 Ma for the new pole); (R2) positive PSV tests, stepwise demagnetization using

### page_10
Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 10.1029/2021JB022881
(cid:38)(cid:68)(cid:85)(cid:87)(cid:72)(cid:86)(cid:76)(cid:68)(cid:81)(cid:3)(cid:38)(cid:82)(cid:82)(cid:85)(cid:71)(cid:76)(cid:81)(cid:68)(cid:87)(cid:72)(cid:3)(cid:82)(cid:81)(cid:3)(cid:56)(cid:81)(cid:76)(cid:87)(cid:3)(cid:54)(cid:83)(cid:75)(cid:72)(cid:85)(cid:72)
Figure 7. Reversal test of specimen-level characteristic remanent magnetizations (Tauxe, 2010). Data with downward directions are compared with upward
directions for a common true mean test.
alternative field and thermal heating, and enough samples (N = 116); (R3) stable magnetic carriers revealed
by combined rock magnetic analysis; (R4) positive fold tests; (R6) positive reversal tests and (R7) no re-
semblance to younger poles. However, our sampling location is rotated with respect to the eastern part of
the Songliao block due to the Triassic left lateral motion along the Nenjiang-Balihan Fault (Figure 1a; Liu
et al., 2017), so that these data fail the fifth R-criteria (R5) of Meert et al. (2020). Above all, we consider the
new pole is reliable for paleolatitudinal reconstructions.
A summary of Permo-Carboniferous paleomagnetic data from North China, Siberia and blocks in the east-
ern CAOB are given in Table 2. The Apparent Polar Wander Path (APWP) for Siberia is adopted from Tors-
vik et al. (2012) and not corrected for inclination shallowing as all data are from igneous rocks. It is notewor-
thy there are only two reliable poles (360 Ma and 250 Ma) and the remainder of the APWP is interpolated.
Another APWP of Siberia (Alternative A; Cocks & Torsvik, 2007) adopted the 275 Ma result of Pisarevsky
et al. (2006), which yields much higher paleolatitudes for Siberia and indicates a separation from Baltica
until 250 Ma. Here we choose not to use this APWP as the 275 Ma pole is similar to younger Triassic poles
and amalgamation between Siberia and Baltica much likely occurred before the Early Permian (Cocks &
Torsvik, 2007; Domeier & Torsvik, 2014; Han et al., 2011). The APWP of North China is adopted from Zhang
et al. (2021), which corrected all clastic poles (data corrected by the original authors are excluded) using a
flattening factor (f) of 0.7 to achieve consistency between coeval clastic and igneous results. Compared to
redbeds, inclination shallowing is less significant in non-redbeds clastic rocks (Bilardello & Kodama, 2010),
which characterized the data set of the CAOB. As a flattening factor of 0.6 has been advocated for the Low-
er Triassic redbeds in North China using anisotropy of remanence (Xue et al., 2021) and E/I corrections
(Zhou, Huang, et al., 2018), here we choose to apply f = 0.7 to correct the non-redbeds clastic data. In this
way, we can achieve a consistent correction in the CAOB and adjacent blocks (see more details in Zhang
et al., 2021). Paleolatitudinal comparison for the different blocks are calculated to a common reference site
at 43°N, 114°E.
Zhao et al. (2020) reported a 283 Ma result from volcanic rocks in the Erguna block and advocated for a
unified North China-Amuria block no later than the Early Permian. These data were obtained from 54
specimens that yielded negative results in PSV tests. They argued that because of similarities to coeval
rocks in Mongolia (Chen et al., 1997; Li et al., 2012; Pruner, 1992; Xu et al., 1997) and the Xilinhot block
(Zhao et al., 2013), PSV was properly averaged. A closer look at those data reveals the following issues. The
22.8° ± 5.7°N expected paleolatitude of Zhao et al. (2020) is much higher than that of Pruner (1992) at
5.1° ± 11.6°N. This inconsistency suggests the results do not average PSV. The results of Chen et al. (1997)
did not fully remove Mesozoic overprints and PSV is unlikely averaged from the limited data set of 25 spec-
imens (Zhang et al., 2021); The results of Li et al. (2012) lack field tests and most demagnetizations display
single component. Besides, they are significantly different from the recent results (Zhang et al., 2021) ob-
tained from the same strata (290 Ma), which have positive fold tests and averaged PSV. The Xilinhot result
(Zhao et al., 2013) spans most of the Permian period (300–252 Ma) and therefore are not strictly coeval with

remagnetization ages and the paleolatitudinal estimates show large uncertainties (5.1°N–19.9°N–34.7°N

for the data set of Zhao et al. (2020) before use in paleogeographic reconstructions.
5.1. A Unified Amuria Block at the Permo-Carboniferous Boundary
The 303 Ma paleopole in this study displays large discrepancy in declination with respect to the 308 Ma
pole ∼from the SMXB of Mongolia block (Figure 8; Zhang et al., 2021), due to vertical-axis rotations of the
sampling localities, as illustrated by the extensive Mesozoic aged strike-slip faulting in the eastern CAOB
(Figures 1a and 1b; Zhao et al., 2015). The above two poles fall along a small circle band (Figure 8), indicat-
ing similar paleolatitudes of 34°N for the Songliao-Jiamusi (33.2° ± 5.4°N) and Mongolia (34.0° ± 3.8°N;
Zhang et al., 2021) blocks at t∼he Permo-Carboniferous boundary (Figure 9; Table 2).
From a geological perspective, the timing of the NHS is controversial with estimates ranging from the Early
Devonian to Early Triassic. Based on stratigraphic analysis and consistent 460–420 Ma magmatic age pop-
ulations from both sides of the NHS, Xu et al. (2015) argued for an Early Devonian aggregation between
the Songliao block and the SMXB. However, this model is challenged by a discovery of the Late Devonian
to Early Carboniferous arc northwest of the NHS (Liu et al., 2019; Feng et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2010). To
the southeast of the NHS, Carboniferous subduction of the Nenjiang Ocean beneath the Songliao-Jiamusi

Plong), latitude and longitude of sampling location (paleopole positions); A , radius of 95% confidence circles of paleopoles; PaLat., paleolatitude; Δλ, error of
95
paleolatitude; L, limestone; C, clastic rocks; V, volcanic rocks; C., comments; Ref., abbreviation of references used in Figures 9 and 10; F, fold test; R, reversal
test; IS, in situ coordinate.
aData obtained from volcanic rocks or having been corrected for inclination shallowing. bData not used in this study but discussed in the text; Apparent Polar
Wander Path of North China is after Zhang et al. (2021) and Siberia after Torsvik et al. (2012).
block was recognized along the northwestern margin of the Songliao basin (Ma et al., 2020). The existence
of a Carboniferous subduction system precludes a pre-Carboniferous closure of the Nenjiang Ocean. Miao
et al. (2004) argued for a Triassic closure based on the geochemistry of the Xinkailing-Kele complex in
the northeastern segment of the NHS. Crystallization ages of the protolith rocks were dated to between
340–292 Ma with metamorphic ages of 216 Ma. The protolith ages were argued to reflect the development
of island arcs and the metamorphic ages to collisional events between the Songliao-Jiamusi and SMXB.
Limited Permo-Triassic subduction records from the NHS provide weak support for the existence of a Nen-
jiang Ocean during this interval. In more recent studies, several lines of evidence from the NHS region
support closure of the Nenjiang Ocean by the Late Carboniferous. These include (a) sedimentary facies
transition from marine strata in the Early Carboniferous to continental facies in the Late Carboniferous (Liu
et al., 2017); (b) the 320 Ma syn-tectonic S-type granites in the Moguqi area (Ma et al., 2020) which imply a
syn-collision tectonic setting; (c) evidence for extension throughout the studied region during the Early Per-
mian and extensive coeval post-orogenic A-type granites (Feng et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2017; Shi et al., 2015;
Wu et al., 2002) and rift-related bimodal volcanic rocks (Zeng et al., 2011).
The western continuation of the Nenjiang suture is represented by the Hegenshan Ophiolites. The Hegen-
shan Ocean was traditionally regarded as a back-arc ocean basin that separated the SMXB from the Xilinhot
block (Eizenhöfer & Zhao, 2018; Liu et al., 2017, 2019; Miao et al., 2008; Xiao et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2015).
Alternatively, it has been interpreted as a continuation of the Nenjiang Ocean, which separated the Songliao
block rather than the Xilinhot block from the SMXB (Figures 1a and 10). Emplacement of the Hegenshan
ophiolite is older than 280 Ma, most likely sometime between 300–335 Ma, based on the unconformity
between the Hegenshan ophiolite and overlying sandstones of the Middle Permian Zhesi Formation (Fig-
ure 1a; Zhou et al., 2015). Thus, the Hegenshan Ocean most likely closed in conjunction with the Nenjiang
Ocean before the Early Permian.

Figure 8. Plot of Permo-Carboniferous paleomagnetic poles of the Siberia, North China, Mongolia (Erguna-SMXB),
Xilinhot and Songliao blocks (Table 2) in 3D-orthogonal projection. Apparent Polar Wander Path of North China
is after Zhang et al. (2021) and Siberia after Torsvik et al. (2012). The 303 Ma pole from the Songliao block falls at a
common small circle with the 308 Ma pole of the Mongolia block, indicating consistent paleolatitudes of two blocks.
In summary, a unified Amuria block was formed no later than the Permo-Carboniferous boundary, situated
at the north side of the PAO with a paleolatitude of 34°N.
∼
5.2. Equatorial Paleopostions of the Xilinhot and North China Blocks
The suture zone between the Songliao and Xilinhot blocks is cryptic due to the irregular and sporadic occur-
rences of the ophiolites at the periphery of the Xilinhot block (Figure 1a; Zhou et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2019).
Paleontological and paleomagnetic evidence do show differences between the two blocks. The Upper Car-
boniferous limestones in the Xilinhot block developed tropical Tethyan phylloid algal-bearing reefs (Yan
et al., 2019) that are similar to North China but distinct from the Boreal-realm characterizing the Mon-
golia and Songliao-Jiamusi blocks (Niu et al., 2021; Shen et al., 2006; Tian et al., 2016; Ueno, 2006; Wang
et al., 2013). The Xilinhot and North China blocks were located at low equatorial latitudes that are signifi-
cantly different from the Songliao-Jiamusi blocks that were located in the horse latitudes ( 33.2° ± 5.4°N;
Figures 9 and 10; Table 2). The distinct paleolatitudes and distribution of Permo-Carbonif∼erous flora and
fauna of the Xilinhot and Songliao blocks negate the assumption of a unified Songliao-Xilinhot block dur-
ing the Late Carboniferous to Early Permian.

Figure 9. Paleolatitudial variation of the Siberia, Mongolia (Erguna-SMXB), Songliao, Xilinhot and North China
blocks during Permo-Carboniferous times (Table 2). Numbers refers to the source references summarized in Table 2.
The 303 Ma pole of the Songliao block falls at the paleolatitudinal variation curve of the Mongolia block. A unified
Amuria block existed since the Permo-Carboniferous boundary. Paleolatitudinal differences for Amuria, Xilinhot and
North China are negligible at 250 Ma, indicative of a unified North China-Amuria block.
5.3. Paleogeographic Reconstruction of the CAOB
Incorporating the available geological evidence, we propose a paleogeographic reconstruction model for
the CAOB in a paleomagnetic reference frame (at 300 Ma; Figure 10). The North China and Xilinhot blocks
were situated at equatorial paleolatitudes. The unified Amuria block was separated from Siberia by the
northeasterly facing MOO and from North China and Xilinhot blocks by the trumpet-shaped PAO. The PAO
opened to the east during the Permian and gradually closed at 250 Ma, when the Xilinhot block finally
amalgamated with North China and Amuria (Figure 9). ∼
In the western part of the CAOB, multiple arc-continent and continent-continent collision events occurred
in the Late Carboniferous to Early Permian, including (a) collision of Kazakhstan and Baltica that resulted
in the closure of the Ural Ocean (Torsvik et al., 2012); (b) arc-continent collision of the East Junggar arc and
Altai block that closed the Ob-Zaisan Ocean (Han & Zhao, 2018 and references therein); (c) continental col-
lision of the Tarim and Kazakhstan-Central Tianshan-Yili blocks that closed out the South Tianshan Ocean
(B. F. Han et al., 2011; Y. G. Han et al., 2019). The East Junggar arc and Altai block bridged the gap between
Amuria and Siberia, located at the hinge of the Mesozoic Mongol-Okhotsk Orocline. The bridge negates a
cut-through seaway that connected the MOO and PAO during Permo-Triassic times and reconciles paleo-
magnetism and geological data as Mesozoic oceanic strata are absent in this area (Bazhenov et al., 2016).
The trapped Junggar oceanic crust was progressively destroyed in the Permian accompanied by intra-conti-
nental deformation (Yi et al., 2015).
6. Conclusions
We carried out the first integrated paleomagnetic and geochronologic study on Upper Carboniferous to
Upper Permian volcanic-sedimentary sequences from the western margin of the Songliao block. Rock mag-
netic analyses revealed that low coercivity PSD to MD magnetite is the dominant magnetic carriers of the
Permian sandstones and PSD magnetite for the 313–292 Ma volcanic rocks from the Dashizhai Formation.
Well-isolated ChRMs are exclusively obtained from the volcanic rocks (116 specimens from 13 sites), and
the mean direction is Dg/Ig = 70.6°/−77.5°, k = 4.8, α = 21.2° before and Ds/Is = 20.6°/−46.6°, k = 55.7,
